nodes.name: Diophantine inequality problem
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be a set of integers, let $\varepsilon$ be a positive parameter, and let $L$ be an $m$-by-$d$ real matrix. One might then ask whether there are infinitely many solutions to \begin{equation} \Vert L\mathbf{a}\Vert_{\infty}\leqslant \varepsilon \end{equation} \noindent in which all of the coordinates of $\mathbf{a}$ lie in $A$.
nodes.statement_short: Do there exist infinitely many $\mathbf{a}\in A^d$ with $\Vert L\mathbf{a}\Vert_\infty\le\varepsilon$?

nodes.name: General diophantine inequality
nodes.statement: \Vert L\mathbf{a}\Vert_{\infty}\leqslant \varepsilon
nodes.label: the general inequality

nodes.name: Example of Möbius orthogonality
nodes.statement: Let $\theta_1,\dots,\theta _s \in \mathbb{R}$ be distinct irrational numbers, let $N$ be an integer parameter, and let $f_1,f_2,\dots,f_{s+1}: \{ 1,\dots,N\} \longrightarrow [-1,1]$ be arbitrary $1$-bounded functions. Then \begin{equation} \frac{1}{N^2} \sum\limits_{\substack{x,d \in \mathbb{Z} \\ 1 \leqslant x \leqslant N}} \mu(x) f_1(x+d)\Big (\prod\limits_{i=2}^{s+1} f_i([x + \theta_{i-1} d]) \Big ) = o(1) \end{equation} \noindent as $N \rightarrow \infty$, where $\mu$ denotes the M\"{o}bius function and $[x] : = \lfloor x + \frac{1}{2}\rfloor$ is the nearest integer to $x$. The $o(1)$ error term may depend on the numbers $\theta_1,\dots,\theta_s$ but is independent of the choice of functions $f_1,\dots,f_{s+1}$.\\
nodes.statement_short: Möbius correlations with irrational-dilate patterns $[x+\theta_i d]$ vanish: the average is $o(1)$.
assumptions: Let $\theta_1,\dots,\theta _s \in \mathbb{R}$ be distinct irrational numbers, let $N$ be an integer parameter, and let $f_1,f_2,\dots,f_{s+1}: \{ 1,\dots,N\} \longrightarrow [-1,1]$ be arbitrary $1$-bounded functions.
conclusions: Then \begin{equation} \frac{1}{N^2} \sum\limits_{\substack{x,d \in \mathbb{Z} \\ 1 \leqslant x \leqslant N}} \mu(x) f_1(x+d)\Big (\prod\limits_{i=2}^{s+1} f_i([x + \theta_{i-1} d]) \Big ) = o(1) \end{equation} \noindent as $N \rightarrow \infty$, where $\mu$ denotes the M\"{o}bius function and $[x] : = \lfloor x + \frac{1}{2}\rfloor$ is the nearest integer to $x$. The $o(1)$ error term may depend on the numbers $\theta_1,\dots,\theta_s$ but is independent of the choice of functions $f_1,\dots,f_{s+1}$.\\
nodes.label: Corollary irrational szem mobius

nodes.name: Möbius irrational pattern average
nodes.statement: \frac{1}{N^2} \sum\limits_{\substack{x,d \in \mathbb{Z} \\ 1 \leqslant x \leqslant N}} \mu(x) f_1(x+d)\Big (\prod\limits_{i=2}^{s+1} f_i([x + \theta_{i-1} d]) \Big ) = o(1)

nodes.name: Davenport-Heilbronn theorem
nodes.statement: For example, if $A$ is the set of squares, it was shown by Davenport and Heilbronn in \cite{DaHe46} that there are infinitely many solutions to (\ref{the general inequality}) for $m=1$ and $d=5$, i.e. infinitely many solutions to \begin{equation} \vert \lambda_1 n_1^2 + \lambda_2 n_2^2 + \lambda_3 n_3^2 + \lambda_4 n_4^2 + \lambda_5 n_5^2 \vert \leqslant \varepsilon, \end{equation} provided the coefficients $\lambda_i$ are non-zero, not all of the same sign, and not all in pairwise rational ratio.
nodes.statement_short: Five squares: $|\sum\lambda_i n_i^2|\le\varepsilon$ has infinitely many solutions for suitable irrational $\lambda_i$.
assumptions: the coefficients $\lambda_i$ are non-zero, not all of the same sign, and not all in pairwise rational ratio
conclusions: there are infinitely many solutions to (\ref{the general inequality}) for $m=1$ and $d=5$

nodes.name: Quadratic diophantine inequality in five squares
nodes.statement: \vert \lambda_1 n_1^2 + \lambda_2 n_2^2 + \lambda_3 n_3^2 + \lambda_4 n_4^2 + \lambda_5 n_5^2 \vert \leqslant \varepsilon,
nodes.label: eq squares

nodes.name: Baker's theorem on linear inequalities in three primes
nodes.statement: A result first claimed in \cite{Ba67} by A. Baker\footnote{In fact Baker proved a slightly different result, writing in \cite{Ba67} that the result we quote here followed easily from the then-existing methods.} states that for any fixed positive $\varepsilon$ there exist infinitely many triples of primes $(p_1,p_2,p_3)$ satisfying \begin{equation} \vert \lambda_1p_1 + \lambda_2p_2 + \lambda_3 p_3\vert \leqslant \varepsilon, \end{equation} \noindent assuming again that the coefficients $\lambda_i$ are non-zero, not all of the same sign, and not all in pairwise rational ratio.
nodes.statement_short: Infinitely many prime triples satisfy $|\lambda_1p_1+\lambda_2p_2+\lambda_3p_3|\le\varepsilon$.
assumptions: the coefficients $\lambda_i$ are non-zero, not all of the same sign, and not all in pairwise rational ratio
conclusions: for any fixed positive $\varepsilon$ there exist infinitely many triples of primes $(p_1,p_2,p_3)$ satisfying

nodes.name: Linear inequality in three primes
nodes.statement: \vert \lambda_1p_1 + \lambda_2p_2 + \lambda_3 p_3\vert \leqslant \varepsilon,
nodes.label: the type of inequality we're talking about

nodes.name: Big-O notation convention
nodes.statement: We will use standard asymptotic notation $O$, $o$, and $\Omega$. We do not, as is sometimes the convention, for a function $f$ and a positive function $g$ choose to write $f = O(g)$ if there exists a constant $C$ such that $\vert f(N)\vert \leqslant C g(N) $ \emph{for $N$ sufficiently large}. Rather we require the inequality to hold for all $N$ in some pre-specified range.
nodes.statement_short: $O,o,\Omega$ notation, with $f=O(g)$ required to hold on the whole pre-specified range.

nodes.name: Negative asymptotic symbols convention
nodes.statement: It will be a convenient shorthand to use these symbols in conjunction with minus signs. So, by convention, we determine that expressions such as $-O(1), -o(1), -\Omega(1)$ are negative, e.g. $N^{-\Omega(1)}$ refers to a term $N^{-c}$, where $c$ is some positive quantity bounded away from $0$ as the asymptotic parameter tends to infinity.

nodes.name: Vinogradov symbol
nodes.statement: It will also be convenient to use the Vinogradov symbol $\ll$, where for a function $f$ and a positive function $g$ we write $f\ll g$ if and only if $f = O(g)$.

nodes.name: Asymptotic equivalence symbol
nodes.statement: We write $f\asymp g$ if $f\ll g$ and $g\ll f$.

nodes.name: Kappa notation
nodes.statement: We also adopt the $\kappa$ notation from \cite{GT10}: $\kappa(x)$ denotes any quantity that tends to zero as $x$ tends to zero, with the exact value being permitted to change from line to line.

nodes.name: Subscripted implied constants
nodes.statement: If an implied constant depends on other parameters, we will denote these by subscripts, e.g. $O_{c,C,\varepsilon}(1)$, or $f\asymp_{\varepsilon} g$.

nodes.name: $o_\rho(1)$ notation
nodes.statement: By notation such as $o_\rho(1)$ we mean a term which tends to zero as the asymptotic parameter tends to infinity with $\rho$ fixed.

nodes.name: Discrete interval [N]
nodes.statement: If $N$ is a natural number, we use $[N]$ to denote $\{n\in \mathbb{N}:n\leqslant N\}$, whereas $[1,N]$ will be reserved for the closed real interval.

nodes.name: Nearest integer and distance to nearest integer
nodes.statement: For $x \in \mathbb{R}$, we write $[x]: = \lfloor x+\frac{1}{2}\rfloor$ for the nearest integer to $x$, and $\Vert x \Vert$ for $\vert x - [x] \vert$.

nodes.name: Torus norm
nodes.statement: For $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^m$, we let $\Vert \mathbf{x}\Vert_{\mathbb{R}^m/\mathbb{Z}^m}$ denote $\sup_i \vert x_i - [x_i]\vert$.

nodes.name: Distance between sets
nodes.statement: If $X,Y\subset\mathbb{R}^d$ for some $d$, we define \[\operatorname{dist}(X,Y): = \inf\limits_{x\in X, y\in Y} \Vert x - y\Vert_{\infty}.\]

nodes.name: Distance between sets of matrices
nodes.statement: By identifying sets of $m$-by-$d$ matrices with subsets of $\mathbb{R}^{md}$ (by identifying the coefficients of the matrices with coordinates in $\mathbb{R}^{md}$), we may also define $\operatorname{dist}(X,Y)$ when $X$ and $Y$ are sets of matrices of the same dimensions.

nodes.name: Max-coefficient norm of a matrix
nodes.statement: The norm $\Vert L\Vert_\infty$ will refer to the maximum absolute value of the coefficients of this matrix.

nodes.name: Dual linear map
nodes.statement: We use the notation $L^*: (\mathbb{R}^m)^* \longrightarrow (\mathbb{R}^d)^*$ for the dual linear map between the dual spaces.

nodes.name: Annihilator
nodes.statement: For a set $U \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ we use $U^{0}$ to denote the annihilator of $U$, i.e. the set of all $f$ in the dual space $(\mathbb{R}^d)^*$ for which $f|_U \equiv 0$.

nodes.name: Topological boundary
nodes.statement: We let $\partial(X)$ denote the topological boundary of a set $X \subset \mathbb{R}^d$.

nodes.name: Dilate of a set
nodes.statement: Given $S \subset \mathbb{R}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, we let $\lambda S: = \{ x \in \mathbb{R}: \exists s \in S \, \text{for which} \, \lambda s = x\}.$

nodes.name: Indicator function
nodes.statement: If $A$ and $B$ are two sets with $A\subseteq B$, we let $1_A:B\longrightarrow \{0,1\}$ denote the indicator function of $A$.

nodes.name: Exponential shorthand e(θ)
nodes.statement: For $\theta \in \mathbb{R}$ we also adopt the standard shorthand $e(\theta)$ to mean $e^{2\pi i \theta}$.

nodes.name: Subvector notation
nodes.statement: In Section \ref{section General proof of the real variable von Neumann Theorem}, if $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and if $a$ and $b$ are two subscripts with $1\leqslant a\leqslant b\leqslant d$, we use the notation $\mathbf{x_a^b}$ to denote the vector $(x_a,x_{a+1},\dots,x_{b})^T \in \mathbb{R}^{b-a+1}$.

nodes.name: Generalised von Neumann Theorem for rational forms (non-quantitative)
nodes.statement: Let $m,d$ be natural numbers, satisfying $d\geqslant m+2$. Let $L$ be an $m$-by-$d$ real matrix with integer coefficients, with rank $m$. Suppose that there does not exist any non-zero row-vector in the row-space of $L$ that has two or fewer non-zero coordinates. Then there is some natural number $s$ at most $d-2$ that satisfies the following. Let $N$ be an integer parameter, let $f_1,\dots,f_d:[N]\longrightarrow [-1,1]$ be arbitrary functions, and suppose that \[ \min_j \Vert f_j\Vert_{U^{s+1}[N]} \leqslant \rho \] for some parameter $\rho$ in the range $0<\rho \leqslant 1$. Then $$\frac{1}{N^{d-m}}\sum\limits_{\substack{\mathbf{n}\in [N]^d\\ L\mathbf{n} = \mathbf{0}}} \prod\limits_{j=1}^d f_j(n_j) \ll_L \rho^{\Omega(1)} + o_\rho(1)$$ as $N\rightarrow \infty$.
nodes.statement_short: For integer $L$ with no 2-sparse row-space vector, weighted solution counts of $L\mathbf{n}=0$ are controlled by $U^{s+1}$ norms.
assumptions: Let $m,d$ be natural numbers, satisfying $d\geqslant m+2$. Let $L$ be an $m$-by-$d$ real matrix with integer coefficients, with rank $m$. Suppose that there does not exist any non-zero row-vector in the row-space of $L$ that has two or fewer non-zero coordinates.
conclusions: Then there is some natural number $s$ at most $d-2$ that satisfies the following. Let $N$ be an integer parameter, let $f_1,\dots,f_d:[N]\longrightarrow [-1,1]$ be arbitrary functions, and suppose that \[ \min_j \Vert f_j\Vert_{U^{s+1}[N]} \leqslant \rho \] for some parameter $\rho$ in the range $0<\rho \leqslant 1$. Then $$\frac{1}{N^{d-m}}\sum\limits_{\substack{\mathbf{n}\in [N]^d\\ L\mathbf{n} = \mathbf{0}}} \prod\limits_{j=1}^d f_j(n_j) \ll_L \rho^{\Omega(1)} + o_\rho(1)$$ as $N\rightarrow \infty$.
nodes.label: Linear equations in bounded functions non quantitative

nodes.name: Necessity of the condition d ≥ m+2
nodes.statement: Regarding the condition $d \geqslant m+2$, if $L$ has rank $m$ and $d \leqslant m+1$ then in fact, as follows Gaussian elimination, there must always exist a non-zero vector in the row space of $L$ with two or fewer non-zero coordinates. Thus, the condition $d \geqslant m+2$ is a necessary one if the coordinates $\ker L$ are to be suitably independent.
nodes.statement_short: If $d\le m+1$, Gaussian elimination gives a row-space vector with at most two non-zero coordinates.

nodes.name: Theorem 1.2 is implicit in Green-Tao
nodes.statement: \emph{Theorem \ref{Linear equations in bounded functions non quantitative} is implicit in \cite{GT10}, but there is no explicit such statement presented there, as those authors were focused on results over the primes. We will describe how to extract Theorem \ref{Linear equations in bounded functions non quantitative} from the arguments of \cite{GT10}, but we postpone this task until Section \ref{section Reductions}, as at that point we will also introduce a quantitative version (this will be Theorem \ref{Linear equations in bounded functions}).}

nodes.name: Gowers norms control diophantine inequalities (non-quantitative)
nodes.statement: Let $m,d$ be natural numbers, satisfying $d\geqslant m+2$, and let $\varepsilon$ be a positive parameter. Let $L:\mathbb{R}^d \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^m$ be an $m$-by-$d$ real matrix, with rank $m$. Suppose that there does not exist any non-zero row-vector in the row-space of $L$ that has two or fewer non-zero coordinates. Then there is some natural number $s$ at most $d-2$, independent of $\varepsilon$, such that the following is true. Let $N$ be an integer parameter and let $f_1,\dots,f_d:[N]\longrightarrow [-1,1]$ be arbitrary functions, and suppose that \[ \min_j \Vert f_j \Vert_{U^{s+1}[N]} \leqslant \rho,\] for some parameter $\rho$ in the range $0<\rho \leqslant 1$. Then \[ \Big\vert \frac{1}{N^{d-m}}\sum\limits_{\substack{\mathbf{n} \in [N]^d \\ \Vert L \mathbf{n} \Vert_\infty \leqslant \varepsilon}} \Big( \prod\limits_{j=1}^d f_j(n_j) \Big)\Big\vert \ll_{L,\varepsilon} \rho^{\Omega(1)} + o_{\rho,L}(1)\] as $N\rightarrow \infty$.
nodes.statement_short: For real non-degenerate $L$, weighted counts of $\Vert L\mathbf{n}\Vert_\infty\le\varepsilon$ are bounded by $\rho^{\Omega(1)}+o(1)$ when some $\Vert f_j\Vert_{U^{s+1}}\le\rho$.
assumptions: Let $m,d$ be natural numbers, satisfying $d\geqslant m+2$, and let $\varepsilon$ be a positive parameter. Let $L:\mathbb{R}^d \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^m$ be an $m$-by-$d$ real matrix, with rank $m$. Suppose that there does not exist any non-zero row-vector in the row-space of $L$ that has two or fewer non-zero coordinates.
conclusions: Then there is some natural number $s$ at most $d-2$, independent of $\varepsilon$, such that the following is true. Let $N$ be an integer parameter and let $f_1,\dots,f_d:[N]\longrightarrow [-1,1]$ be arbitrary functions, and suppose that \[ \min_j \Vert f_j \Vert_{U^{s+1}[N]} \leqslant \rho,\] for some parameter $\rho$ in the range $0<\rho \leqslant 1$. Then \[ \Big\vert \frac{1}{N^{d-m}}\sum\limits_{\substack{\mathbf{n} \in [N]^d \\ \Vert L \mathbf{n} \Vert_\infty \leqslant \varepsilon}} \Big( \prod\limits_{j=1}^d f_j(n_j) \Big)\Big\vert \ll_{L,\varepsilon} \rho^{\Omega(1)} + o_{\rho,L}(1)\] as $N\rightarrow \infty$.
nodes.label: much easier to state

nodes.name: Corollary 1.4 implies Theorem 1.2 for integer L
nodes.statement: Firstly, note that if $L$ has integer coefficients then, by picking $\varepsilon$ small enough, Corollary \ref{much easier to state} immediately implies Theorem \ref{Linear equations in bounded functions non quantitative}, sine the inequality $\Vert L\mathbf{n}\Vert_\infty \leqslant \varepsilon$ is only satisfied if $L\mathbf{n} = \mathbf{0}$.

nodes.name: Corollary 1.4 under a U^{d-1} hypothesis
nodes.statement: Next, due to the nested property of Gowers norms (see Appendix \ref{sec.Gowers norms}), one sees that Corollary \ref{much easier to state} may be fruitfully applied under the hypothesis $\min_j\Vert f_j\Vert_{U^{d-1}[N]} \leqslant \rho$.

nodes.name: Three-term irrational AP
nodes.section: 1.4 Fourier uniform sets and other examples
nodes.statement_short: Applies Corollary 1.4 to $L=(1,-\sqrt2,-1+\sqrt2)$, counting irrational 3-term APs $(x,x+d,[x+\sqrt2 d])$ in Fourier-uniform sets.
nodes.label: example three term irrational AP

nodes.name: Three-term irrational AP bound
nodes.statement: \Big\vert\frac{1}{N^2}\sum\limits_{\substack{n_1,n_2,n_3\leqslant N\\ \vert n_1 - \sqrt{2}n_2 + (-1+\sqrt{2})n_3\vert\leqslant \varepsilon} }f_1(n_1)f_2(n_2)f_3(n_3)\Big\vert \ll_\varepsilon \rho^{\Omega(1)} +o_{\rho}(1)
nodes.section: 1.4 Fourier uniform sets and other examples
nodes.label: three term Ap eq explicit

nodes.name: Irrational three-term AP count T
nodes.statement: Then for any three functions $f_1,f_2,f_3:[N]\longrightarrow [-1,1]$, we make the definition \begin{equation} T(f_1,f_2,f_3):=\frac{1}{N^2}\sum\limits_{x,d\in \mathbb{Z}} f_3(x)f_2(x+d)f_1([x+\sqrt{2} d]). \end{equation}
nodes.section: 1.4 Fourier uniform sets and other examples

nodes.name: Definition of T(f1,f2,f3)
nodes.statement: T(f_1,f_2,f_3):=\frac{1}{N^2}\sum\limits_{x,d\in \mathbb{Z}} f_3(x)f_2(x+d)f_1([x+\sqrt{2} d]).
nodes.section: 1.4 Fourier uniform sets and other examples

nodes.name: Möbius orthogonality
nodes.statement: Let $m,d$ be natural numbers satisfying $d\geqslant m+2$, and let $\varepsilon$ be a positive parameter. Let $L:\mathbb{R}^d \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^m$ be an $m$-by-$d$ real matrix, with rank $m$. Suppose that there does not exist any non-zero row-vector in the row-space of $L$ that has two or fewer non-zero coordinates. Let $\mu$ denote the M\"{o}bius function and let $N$ be an integer parameter. Then, for any bounded functions $f_2,\dots,f_d:[N]\longrightarrow [-1,1]$, \[ \sum\limits_{ \substack{\mathbf{n} \in [N]^d\\ \Vert L\mathbf{n}\Vert_\infty \leqslant \varepsilon}} \mu(n_1) \Big(\prod\limits_{j=2}^d f_j(n_j)\Big)= o_{L,\varepsilon}(N^{d-m})\] as $N\rightarrow \infty$. The same is true with $\mu$ replaced by the Liouville function $\lambda$.
nodes.section: 1.4 Fourier uniform sets and other examples
nodes.statement_short: The Möbius (or Liouville) function has $o(N^{d-m})$ correlation over solutions of non-degenerate real linear inequalities.
assumptions: Let $m,d$ be natural numbers satisfying $d\geqslant m+2$, and let $\varepsilon$ be a positive parameter. Let $L:\mathbb{R}^d \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^m$ be an $m$-by-$d$ real matrix, with rank $m$. Suppose that there does not exist any non-zero row-vector in the row-space of $L$ that has two or fewer non-zero coordinates. nodes.name: Solution count T^L_{F,G,N}
nodes.statement: Let $N,m,d$ be natural numbers, and let $L:\mathbb{R}^d \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^m$ be a linear map. Let $F:\mathbb{R}^d\longrightarrow [0,1]$ and $G:\mathbb{R}^m\longrightarrow [0,1]$ be two functions, with $F$ supported on $[-N,N]^d$ and $G$ compactly supported. Let $f_1,\dots,f_d:[N]\longrightarrow [-1,1]$ be arbitrary functions. We define \begin{equation} T_{F,G,N}^L(f_1,\dots,f_d) := \frac{1}{N^{d-m}}\sum\limits_{\mathbf{n}\in \mathbb{Z}^d}\Big(\prod\limits_{j=1}^d f_j(n_j)\Big)F(\mathbf{n})G(L\mathbf{n}). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Normalised weighted count of $\mathbf{n}\in\mathbb{Z}^d$ with cut-offs $F(\mathbf{n})$ and $G(L\mathbf{n})$.

nodes.name: Rational dimension, rational map, purely irrational
nodes.statement: Let $m$ and $d$ be natural numbers, with $d\geqslant m+1$. Let $L:\mathbb{R}^d\longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^m$ be a surjective linear map. Let $u$ denote the largest integer for which there exists a surjective linear map $\Theta:\mathbb{R}^m \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^u$ for which $\Theta L (\mathbb{Z}^d) \subseteq \mathbb{Z}^u$. We call $u$ the \emph{rational dimension} of $L$, and we call any map $\Theta$ with the above property a \emph{rational map} for $L$. We say that $L$ is \emph{purely irrational} if $u=0$.
nodes.statement_short: The rational dimension of $L$ is the largest $u$ with a surjection $\Theta$ to $\mathbb{R}^u$ mapping $L(\mathbb{Z}^d)$ into $\mathbb{Z}^u$.
nodes.label: Definition rational space

nodes.name: A 2-by-4 matrix of rational dimension 1
nodes.statement: For example, suppose that $L:\mathbb{R}^4 \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^2$ is the linear map represented by the matrix \[ L: = \left(\begin{matrix} 1 & 0 & -\sqrt{2} & -\sqrt{3} + 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 5\sqrt{2} & 5\sqrt{3} \end{matrix} \right).\] If $\Theta:\mathbb{R}^2 \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}$ is given by the matrix \[ \Theta:= \Big(\begin{matrix} 5 & 1 \end{matrix} \Big),\] then $\Theta L (\mathbb{Z}^4) \subseteq \mathbb{Z}$, and in fact $\Theta L (\mathbb{Z}^4) = \mathbb{Z}$. So the rational dimension of $L$ is at least $1$. But the rational dimension of $L$ cannot be $2$, as if there were a surjective map $\Theta:\mathbb{R}^2 \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^2$ such that $\Theta L (\mathbb{Z}^4) \subseteq \mathbb{Z}^2$ then $L(\mathbb{Z}^4)$ would be a subset of a $2$-dimensional lattice, which it is not. So the rational dimension of $L$ is equal to $1$.
nodes.statement_short: A $2\times4$ matrix with $\Theta=(5\ 1)$ shows rational dimension exactly $1$.

nodes.name: Invariance of the kernel of rational maps
nodes.statement: Let $m$ and $d$ be natural numbers, with $d\geqslant m+1$. Let $L:\mathbb{R}^d\longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^m$ be a surjective linear map, and let $u$ be the rational dimension of $L$. Then, if $\Theta_1,\Theta_2: \mathbb{R}^m \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^u$ are two rational maps for $L$, $\ker \Theta_1 = \ker \Theta_2$.
assumptions: Let $m$ and $d$ be natural numbers, with $d\geqslant m+1$. Let $L:\mathbb{R}^d\longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^m$ be a surjective linear map, and let $u$ be the rational dimension of $L$.
conclusions: Then, if $\Theta_1,\Theta_2: \mathbb{R}^m \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^u$ are two rational maps for $L$, $\ker \Theta_1 = \ker \Theta_2$.
nodes.label: Lemma invariant space

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.3
nodes.statement: Suppose that $\Theta_1,\Theta_2:\mathbb{R}^m \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^u$ are two rational maps for $L$ for which $\ker \Theta_1 \neq \ker \Theta_2$. Then consider the map $(\Theta_1,\Theta_2):\mathbb{R}^m\longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^{2u}.$ The kernel of this map has dimension at most $m-u-1$, as it is the intersection of two different subspaces of dimension $m-u$. Therefore the image has dimension at least $u+1$. Also, $((\Theta_1,\Theta_2) \circ L ) (\mathbb{Z}^d) \subseteq \mathbb{Z}^{2u}. $ Let $\Phi$ be any surjective map from $\operatorname{im} ((\Theta_1,\Theta_2))$ to $\mathbb{R}^{u+1}$ for which $\Phi(\mathbb{Z}^{2u}\cap\operatorname{im} ((\Theta_1,\Theta_2))) \subseteq\mathbb{Z}^{u+1}$. Then $\Phi \circ (\Theta_1,\Theta_2):\mathbb{R}^m \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^{u+1}$ is surjective and $(\Phi \circ (\Theta_1,\Theta_2) \circ L)(\mathbb{Z}^d) \subseteq \mathbb{Z}^{u+1}$. This contradicts the definition of $u$ as the rational dimension.
nodes.statement_short: If two rational maps had different kernels, combining them would give a rational map to $\mathbb{R}^{u+1}$, contradicting maximality of $u$.

nodes.name: Rational complexity
nodes.statement: Let $m$ and $d$ be natural numbers, with $d\geqslant m+1$. Let $L:\mathbb{R}^d\longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^m$ be a surjective linear map, and let $u$ denote the rational dimension of $L$. We say that $L$ has \emph{rational complexity at most $C$} if there exists a map $\Theta$ that is a rational map for $L$ and for which $\Vert \Theta\Vert_\infty \leqslant C$. If $L$ is purely irrational, then $L$ has rational complexity $0$.

nodes.name: Maximal rational dimension
nodes.statement: Let $m$ and $d$ be natural numbers, with $d\geqslant m+1$. Let $L:\mathbb{R}^d\longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^m$ be a surjective linear map, and suppose that $L$ has rational dimension $m$ and rational complexity at most $C$. Then there exists an invertible $m$-by-$m$ matrix $\Theta$ and an $m$-by-$d$ matrix $S$ with integer coefficients such that, as matrices, $\Theta L = S$. Furthermore, $\Vert \Theta\Vert_\infty \leqslant C$.
assumptions: Let $m$ and $d$ be natural numbers, with $d\geqslant m+1$. Let $L:\mathbb{R}^d\longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^m$ be a surjective linear map, and suppose that $L$ has rational dimension $m$ and rational complexity at most $C$.
conclusions: Then there exists an invertible $m$-by-$m$ matrix $\Theta$ and an $m$-by-$d$ matrix $S$ with integer coefficients such that, as matrices, $\Theta L = S$. Furthermore, $\Vert \Theta\Vert_\infty \leqslant C$.
nodes.label: Lemma full rational dimension

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.5
nodes.statement: Let $\Theta:\mathbb{R}^m \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^m$ be a rational map for $L$ for which $\Vert \Theta \Vert_\infty \leqslant C$.
nodes.statement_short: Take a rational map $\Theta$ with $\Vert\Theta\Vert_\infty\le C$.

nodes.name: Heuristic approximation-function expression
nodes.statement: N^{-1}\max \limits_{ \substack{\mathbf{k} \in \mathbb{Z}^m \\ 0 < \Vert \mathbf{k}\Vert_\infty \leqslant X}} \Vert L^T \mathbf{k}\Vert_{\mathbb{R}^d/\mathbb{Z}^d}^{-1},

nodes.name: Approximation function
nodes.statement: Let $m$ and $d$ be natural numbers, with $d\geqslant m+1$. Let $L:\mathbb{R}^d\longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^m$ be a surjective linear map, and let $u$ denote the rational dimension of $L$. Let $\Theta:\mathbb{R}^m\longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^u$ be any rational map for $L$. Suppose that $u\leqslant m-1$. Then we define the \emph{approximation function of $L$}, denoted $A_L:(0,1] \times (0,1]\longrightarrow (0,\infty)$, by \[ A_L(\tau_1,\tau_2) : = \inf\limits_{\substack{\varphi \in (\mathbb{R}^m)^*\\ \operatorname{dist}( \varphi, \Theta^*((\mathbb{R}^u)^*)) \geqslant \tau_1 \\ \Vert \varphi \Vert_\infty \leqslant \tau_2^{-1}} } \operatorname{dist} (L^* \varphi, (\mathbb{Z}^d)^T ),\] where $(\mathbb{Z}^d)^T$ denotes the set of those $\varphi \in (\mathbb{R}^d)^*$ that have integer coordinates with respect to the standard dual basis. If $u = m$, we define\footnote{When $u=m$ we've already seen (Lemma \ref{Lemma full rational dimension}) that $L$ may be transformed into a matrix $S$ with integer coefficients, and thus $L$ is somewhat degenerate from the point of view of diophantine approximation. We define $A_L(\tau_1,\tau_2)$ for such matrices only to avoid having to discuss this special case in the statement of Theorem \ref{Main Theorem chapter 3} later on.} $A_L(\tau_1,\tau_2)$ to be identically equal to $\tau_1$.
nodes.statement_short: $A_L(\tau_1,\tau_2)$ is the least distance of $L^*\varphi$ from integer covectors over $\varphi$ far from rational relations and of size at most $\tau_2^{-1}$.
nodes.label: Definition approximation function

nodes.name: Approximation function is independent of Θ
nodes.statement: Note that Definition \ref{Definition approximation function} is independent of the choice of $\Theta$.
conclusions: Note that Definition \ref{Definition approximation function} is independent of the choice of $\Theta$.

nodes.name: Proof that A_L is independent of Θ
nodes.statement: Indeed, by basic linear algebra $\Theta^*((\mathbb{R}^u)^*) = (\ker \Theta)^{0} $, where $(\ker \Theta)^{0}$ is the annihilator of $\ker \Theta$ (see Section \ref{Section Notation}). By Lemma \ref{Lemma invariant space}, $\ker \Theta$ is independent of the choice of $\Theta$, and therefore so is $(\ker \Theta)^0$.
nodes.statement_short: $\Theta^*((\mathbb{R}^u)^*)=(\ker\Theta)^0$ and $\ker\Theta$ is independent of $\Theta$ by Lemma 2.3.

nodes.name: Approximation function of the three-term AP matrix
nodes.statement: \emph{Suppose that, as a matrix, \begin{equation*} L := \left(\begin{matrix} 1 & -\sqrt{2} & -1 + \sqrt {2}\end{matrix}\right) \end{equation*} as in Example \ref{example three term irrational AP}. Then $L$ is purely irrational, i.e. $u=0$, since its coefficients are not all in rational ratio. Therefore $A_L(\tau_1,\tau_2)$ is equal to \[ \inf\limits_{\substack{k\in \mathbb{R}: \tau_1 \leqslant \vert k\vert \leqslant \tau_2^{-1} }} \max(\Vert k\Vert_{\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}},\Vert -k \sqrt{2}\Vert_{\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}}, \Vert -k+k\sqrt{2}\Vert_{\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}}). \] As we said above, we seek an upper bound on $A_L(\tau_1,\tau_2)^{-1}$. To this end, we claim that, for this particular $L$ and for all $\tau_1,\tau_2 \in (0,1]$, one has \[ A_L(\tau_1,\tau_2) \gg \min (\tau_1,\tau_2).\]} \emph{Indeed, we know that, for all $q \in \mathbb{N}$, $\Vert q \sqrt{2} \Vert_{\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}} \geqslant 1/(10q)$. This is the statement that $\sqrt{2}$ is a badly approximable irrational. The proof is straightforward: if there were some natural number $p$ for which $\vert q\sqrt{2} - p\vert < 1/(10q)$, then \[ 1 \leqslant \vert 2q^{2} - p^2\vert < \frac{\sqrt{2}}{10} + \frac{p}{10q} < \frac{\sqrt{2}}{5} + \frac{1}{10},\] which is a contradiction.} \emph{Suppose first that $\Vert k\Vert_{\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}}\leqslant \tau_2/100$ and $1/2 \leqslant \vert k\vert \leqslant \tau_2^{-1}$. Then, replacing $k$ by $[k]$ (the nearest integer to $k$), we can conclude that} \begin{align*} \max(\Vert -k \sqrt{2}\Vert_{\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}}, \Vert -k+k\sqrt{2}\Vert_{\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}}) &\geqslant \Vert [k] \sqrt{2}\Vert_{\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}} - \frac{\tau_2}{50} \\ & \geqslant \frac{1}{10 [k]} - \frac{\tau_2}{50} \\ & \geqslant\frac{1}{10\tau_2^{-1} + 10} - \frac{\tau_2}{50} \\ &\gg \tau_2. \end{align*} \emph{Otherwise, one has \[ \Vert k\Vert_{\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}} \gg \min(\tau_1,\tau_2).\] Therefore, \[A_L(\tau_1,\tau_2) \gg \min(\tau_1, \tau_2)\] as claimed.}
nodes.statement_short: For $L=(1,-\sqrt2,-1+\sqrt2)$, bad approximability of $\sqrt2$ gives $A_L(\tau_1,\tau_2)\gg\min(\tau_1,\tau_2)$.
nodes.label: Example approx function

nodes.name: Lower bound on the approximation function for the three-term AP matrix
nodes.statement: To this end, we claim that, for this particular $L$ and for all $\tau_1,\tau_2 \in (0,1]$, one has \[ A_L(\tau_1,\tau_2) \gg \min (\tau_1,\tau_2).\]
assumptions: for all $\tau_1,\tau_2 \in (0,1]$
conclusions: \[ A_L(\tau_1,\tau_2) \gg \min (\tau_1,\tau_2).\]

nodes.name: Proof of the claim in Example 2.7
nodes.statement: Indeed, we know that, for all $q \in \mathbb{N}$, $\Vert q \sqrt{2} \Vert_{\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}} \geqslant 1/(10q)$. This is the statement that $\sqrt{2}$ is a badly approximable irrational. The proof is straightforward: if there were some natural number $p$ for which $\vert q\sqrt{2} - p\vert < 1/(10q)$, then \[ 1 \leqslant \vert 2q^{2} - p^2\vert < \frac{\sqrt{2}}{10} + \frac{p}{10q} < \frac{\sqrt{2}}{5} + \frac{1}{10},\] which is a contradiction.} \emph{Suppose first that $\Vert k\Vert_{\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}}\leqslant \tau_2/100$ and $1/2 \leqslant \vert k\vert \leqslant \tau_2^{-1}$. Then, replacing $k$ by $[k]$ (the nearest integer to $k$), we can conclude that} \begin{align*} \max(\Vert -k \sqrt{2}\Vert_{\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}}, \Vert -k+k\sqrt{2}\Vert_{\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}}) &\geqslant \Vert [k] \sqrt{2}\Vert_{\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}} - \frac{\tau_2}{50} \\ & \geqslant \frac{1}{10 [k]} - \frac{\tau_2}{50} \\ & \geqslant\frac{1}{10\tau_2^{-1} + 10} - \frac{\tau_2}{50} \\ &\gg \tau_2. \end{align*} \emph{Otherwise, one has \[ \Vert k\Vert_{\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}} \gg \min(\tau_1,\tau_2).\] Therefore, \[A_L(\tau_1,\tau_2) \gg \min(\tau_1, \tau_2)\] as claimed.
nodes.statement_short: Case split on whether $k$ is near an integer; use that $\sqrt2$ is badly approximable.

nodes.name: √2 is badly approximable
nodes.statement: Indeed, we know that, for all $q \in \mathbb{N}$, $\Vert q \sqrt{2} \Vert_{\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}} \geqslant 1/(10q)$. This is the statement that $\sqrt{2}$ is a badly approximable irrational.
nodes.statement_short: $\Vert q\sqrt2\Vert_{\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}}\ge 1/(10q)$ for all $q\in\mathbb{N}$.
assumptions: for all $q \in \mathbb{N}$
conclusions: $\Vert q \sqrt{2} \Vert_{\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}} \geqslant 1/(10q)$

nodes.name: Proof that √2 is badly approximable
nodes.statement: The proof is straightforward: if there were some natural number $p$ for which $\vert q\sqrt{2} - p\vert < 1/(10q)$, then \[ 1 \leqslant \vert 2q^{2} - p^2\vert < \frac{\sqrt{2}}{10} + \frac{p}{10q} < \frac{\sqrt{2}}{5} + \frac{1}{10},\] which is a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: If $|q\sqrt2-p|<1/(10q)$ then $1\le|2q^2-p^2|<\sqrt2/5+1/10$, a contradiction.

nodes.name: Approximation function for algebraic coefficients
nodes.statement: It is not too difficult to show that if $L$ is an $m$-by-$d$ matrix with rank $m$ and with algebraic coefficients, then \begin{equation} A_L(\tau_1,\tau_2) \gg_L \min(\tau_1,\tau_2^{O_L(1)}), \end{equation} where the $O_L(1)$ term in the exponent depends on the algebraic degree of the coefficients\footnote{One could perhaps remove this dependence by using the Schmidt subspace theorem, though as there are power losses throughout the rest of the argument there does not seem to be a great advantage in doing so.} of $L$.
nodes.statement_short: For algebraic $L$ of rank $m$, $A_L(\tau_1,\tau_2)\gg_L\min(\tau_1,\tau_2^{O_L(1)})$.
assumptions: $L$ is an $m$-by-$d$ matrix with rank $m$ and with algebraic coefficients
conclusions: A_L(\tau_1,\tau_2) \gg_L \min(\tau_1,\tau_2^{O_L(1)}),

nodes.name: Approximation function bound in the algebraic case
nodes.statement: A_L(\tau_1,\tau_2) \gg_L \min(\tau_1,\tau_2^{O_L(1)}),
nodes.label: approximation function in the algebraic case

nodes.name: Approximation function is positive
nodes.statement: For all permissible choices of $L$, $\tau_1$ and $\tau_2$ in Definition \ref{Definition approximation function}, $A_L(\tau_1,\tau_2)$ is positive.
assumptions: For all permissible choices of $L$, $\tau_1$ and $\tau_2$ in Definition \ref{Definition approximation function}
conclusions: $A_L(\tau_1,\tau_2)$ is positive.
nodes.label: claim approximation function is positive

nodes.name: Proof of Claim 2.8
nodes.statement: Let $u$ be the rational dimension of $L$. Without loss of generality we may assume that $u\leqslant m-1$. Then, for all $\varphi \in (\mathbb{R}^m)^* \setminus \Theta^*((\mathbb{R}^u)^*)$ we have that $\operatorname{dist} (L^* \varphi, (\mathbb{Z}^d)^T )> 0$. (If this were not the case then the map $(\Theta,\varphi):\mathbb{R}^m \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^{u+1}$ would contradict the definition of $u$.) Therefore, as the definition of $A_L(\tau_1,\tau_2)$ involves taking the infimum of a positive continuous function over a compact set, $A_L(\tau_1,\tau_2)$ is positive.
nodes.statement_short: $\operatorname{dist}(L^*\varphi,(\mathbb{Z}^d)^T)>0$ off the rational relations; infimum of a positive continuous function over a compact set.

nodes.name: Low-rank variety and uniform low-rank variety
nodes.statement: Let $m,d$ be natural numbers satisfying $d\geqslant m+1$. Let $V_{\operatorname{rank}}(m,d)$ denote the set of all linear maps $L:\mathbb{R}^d \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^m$ whose rank is less than $m$. We call $V_{\operatorname{rank}}(m,d)$ the \emph{low-rank variety}. Let $V_{ \operatorname{rank}}^{\operatorname{unif}}(m,d)$ denote the set of all linear maps $L:\mathbb{R}^d \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^m$ for which there exists a standard basis vector of $\mathbb{R}^d$, say $\mathbf{e_i}$, for which $L|_{\operatorname{span}(\mathbf{e_j}:j\neq i)}$ has rank less than $m$. We call $V_{ \operatorname{rank}}^{\operatorname{unif}}(m,d)$ the \emph{uniform low-rank variety}.
nodes.label: Definition rank variety

nodes.name: Dual degeneracy variety
nodes.statement: Let $m,d$ be natural numbers satisfying $d\geqslant m+2$. Let $\mathbf{e_1}, \dots,\mathbf{e_d}$ denote the standard basis vectors of $\mathbb{R}^d$, and let $\mathbf{e_1^\ast}, \dots,\mathbf{e_d^\ast}$ denote the dual basis of $(\mathbb{R}^d)^\ast$. Then let $V^*_{\operatorname{degen}}(m,d)$ denote the set of all linear maps $L:\mathbb{R}^d \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^m$ for which there exist two indices $i,j \leqslant d$, and some real number $\lambda$, such that $\mathbf{e_i}^* - \lambda \mathbf{e_j}^*$ is non-zero and $(\mathbf{e_i}^* - \lambda \mathbf{e_j}^*) \in L^*((\mathbb{R}^m)^*)$. We call $V^*_{\operatorname{degen}}(m,d)$ the \emph{dual degeneracy variety}.
nodes.statement_short: Maps $L$ whose row space contains a non-zero covector $\mathbf{e_i}^*-\lambda\mathbf{e_j}^*$ with at most two non-zero coordinates.
nodes.label: Definition dual degeneracy variety

nodes.name: Non-degeneracy for equations
nodes.statement: Indeed, for equations, $L$ is non-degenerate if \begin{equation} L \notin V_{\operatorname{rank}}(m,d) \qquad \text{or} \qquad L \notin V_{\operatorname{degen}}^*(m,d). \end{equation}

nodes.name: Non-degeneracy conditions for equations
nodes.statement: L \notin V_{\operatorname{rank}}(m,d) \qquad \text{or} \qquad L \notin V_{\operatorname{degen}}^*(m,d).
nodes.label: conditions for equations

nodes.name: Non-degeneracy for inequalities
nodes.statement: For inequalities, $L$ is non-degenerate if \begin{equation} \operatorname{dist}(L, V_{\operatorname{rank}}^{\operatorname{unif}}(m,d)) \geqslant c \qquad \text{or} \qquad \operatorname{dist}(L,V_{\operatorname{degen}}^*(m,d)) \geqslant c^\prime, \end{equation} for some fixed parameters $c$ and $c^\prime$.

nodes.name: Non-degeneracy conditions for inequalities
nodes.statement: \operatorname{dist}(L, V_{\operatorname{rank}}^{\operatorname{unif}}(m,d)) \geqslant c \qquad \text{or} \qquad \operatorname{dist}(L,V_{\operatorname{degen}}^*(m,d)) \geqslant c^\prime,
nodes.label: conditions for inequalities

nodes.name: Matrix degenerate for inequalities but not equations
nodes.statement: \emph{It may be instructive to consider a matrix such as $$L = \left(\begin{matrix} 1 +N^{-1}& \sqrt{3}+N^{-\frac{1}{2}} & \pi & -\pi+\sqrt{2} \\ 2 & 2\sqrt{3}+N^{-\frac{1}{2}} & -\sqrt{5} & e \end{matrix} \right).$$ We observe that $L$ has rank 2 and $L\notin V_{\operatorname{degen}}^*(2,4)$. If one knew Theorem \ref{Linear equations in bounded functions non quantitative} and the conditions (\ref{conditions for equations}), then one might perhaps have hoped to apply the theory of Gowers norms to bound the number of solutions to inequalities given by $L$. However, by considering perturbations of the first two columns, we see that $\operatorname{dist}(L,V_{\operatorname{degen}}^*(2,4))=o(1)$ as $N\rightarrow \infty$. Indeed, one may perturb $L$ by $O(N^{-1/2})$ such that there is a vector $(0,0,x_3,x_4)$ in the row space. So, despite the fact that $L$ is non-degenerate from the point of view of equations, $L$ \emph{is} degenerate from the point of view of inequalities and the conditions (\ref{conditions for inequalities}). Thus, our main theorem on inequalities will not apply to this $L$. } \emph{Furthermore, we have another result (Theorem \ref{Converse to main theorem} below) which shows that one cannot possibly use Gowers norms to control inequalities given by such an $L$. Therefore, whatever methods we use to prove Theorem \ref{Main Theorem chapter 3}, these methods must necessarily break down when applied to this example.}\\
nodes.statement_short: An $N$-dependent matrix non-degenerate for equations but within $o(1)$ of $V^*_{\operatorname{degen}}(2,4)$.
nodes.label: Example bad behaviour

nodes.name: Main Theorem
nodes.statement: Let $m,d$ be natural numbers, satisfying $d\geqslant m+2$, and let $\varepsilon , c, C, C^\prime$ be positive reals. Let $N$ be an integer parameter and let $L = L(N):\mathbb{R}^d \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^m$ be a surjective linear map that satisfies $\Vert L\Vert_\infty\leqslant C$. Let $A_L:(0,1]\times (0,1]\longrightarrow (0,\infty)$ be the approximation function of $L$. Suppose further that $\operatorname{dist}(L,V_{\operatorname{rank}}^{\operatorname{unif}}(m,d)) \geqslant c$, that $\operatorname{dist}(L,V^*_{\operatorname{degen}}(m,d))\geqslant c^\prime$, and that $L$ has rational complexity at most $C^\prime$. Then there exists a natural number $s$ at most $d-2$, independent of $\varepsilon$, such that the following is true. Let $F:\mathbb{R}^d\longrightarrow [0,1]$ be the indicator function of $[1,N]^d$, and let $G:\mathbb{R}^m\longrightarrow [0,1]$ be the indicator function of a convex domain contained in $[-\varepsilon, \varepsilon]^m$. Let $f_1,\dots,f_d:[N]\longrightarrow [-1,1]$ be arbitrary functions, and suppose that \[ \min_j \Vert f_j\Vert_{U^{s+1}[N]} \leqslant \rho,\] for some parameter $\rho$ in the range $0<\rho \leqslant 1$. Then \begin{equation} T^{L}_{F,G,N}(f_1,\dots,f_{d})\ll_{c,c^\prime,C,C^\prime,\varepsilon} \rho^{\Omega(1)} + o_{\rho,A_L,c,c^\prime,C,C^\prime}(1) \end{equation} as $N\rightarrow \infty$. The $o_{\rho,A_L,c,c^\prime,C,C^\prime}(1)$ term may be bounded above by \[ N^{-\Omega(1)}\rho^{-O(1)} A_L(\Omega_{c,c^\prime,C,C^{\prime}}(1),\rho)^{-1}.\]
nodes.section: 2.4 The main theorem and a partial converse
nodes.statement_short: Quantitative control of $T^L_{F,G,N}$ by Gowers norms for non-degenerate real $L$, with error depending on the approximation function $A_L$.
assumptions: Let $m,d$ be natural numbers, satisfying $d\geqslant m+2$, and let $\varepsilon , c, C, C^\prime$ be positive reals. Let $N$ be an integer parameter and let $L = L(N):\mathbb{R}^d \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^m$ be a surjective linear map that satisfies $\Vert L\Vert_\infty\leqslant C$. Let $A_L:(0,1]\times (0,1]\longrightarrow (0,\infty)$ be the approximation function of $L$. Suppose further that $\operatorname{dist}(L,V_{\operatorname{rank}}^{\operatorname{unif}}(m,d)) \geqslant c$, that $\operatorname{dist}(L,V^*_{\operatorname{degen}}(m,d))\geqslant c^\prime$, and that $L$ has rational complexity at most $C^\prime$.
conclusions: Then there exists a natural number $s$ at most $d-2$, independent of $\varepsilon$, such that the following is true. Let $F:\mathbb{R}^d\longrightarrow [0,1]$ be the indicator function of $[1,N]^d$, and let $G:\mathbb{R}^m\longrightarrow [0,1]$ be the indicator function of a convex domain contained in $[-\varepsilon, \varepsilon]^m$. Let $f_1,\dots,f_d:[N]\longrightarrow [-1,1]$ be arbitrary functions, and suppose that \[ \min_j \Vert f_j\Vert_{U^{s+1}[N]} \leqslant \rho,\] for some parameter $\rho$ in the range $0<\rho \leqslant 1$. Then \begin{equation} T^{L}_{F,G,N}(f_1,\dots,f_{d})\ll_{c,c^\prime,C,C^\prime,\varepsilon} \rho^{\Omega(1)} + o_{\rho,A_L,c,c^\prime,C,C^\prime}(1) \end{equation} as $N\rightarrow \infty$. The $o_{\rho,A_L,c,c^\prime,C,C^\prime}(1)$ term may be bounded above by \[ N^{-\Omega(1)}\rho^{-O(1)} A_L(\Omega_{c,c^\prime,C,C^{\prime}}(1),\rho)^{-1}.\]
nodes.label: Main Theorem chapter 3

nodes.name: Main theorem bound
nodes.statement: T^{L}_{F,G,N}(f_1,\dots,f_{d})\ll_{c,c^\prime,C,C^\prime,\varepsilon} \rho^{\Omega(1)} + o_{\rho,A_L,c,c^\prime,C,C^\prime}(1)
nodes.section: 2.4 The main theorem and a partial converse
nodes.label: main equation chapter 3 theorem

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 1.4 from the Main Theorem
nodes.statement: Firstly, since $A_L(\Omega_{c,C}(1),\rho)^{-1}$ is finite (by Claim \ref{claim approximation function is positive}), Theorem \ref{Main Theorem chapter 3} immediately implies Corollary \ref{much easier to state} (this was the qualitative statement around which we structured Section \ref{Sec introduction}).
nodes.section: 2.4 The main theorem and a partial converse
nodes.statement_short: $A_L(\cdot,\rho)^{-1}$ is finite by Claim 2.8, so Theorem 2.12 gives Corollary 1.4.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 2.13
nodes.statement: Secondly, from (\ref{approximation function in the algebraic case}), or rather from our full quantitative version in Lemma \ref{Lemma algebraic coeffs implies gen appr}, we have another corollary for matrices $L$ with algebraic coefficients.
nodes.section: 2.4 The main theorem and a partial converse
nodes.statement_short: Insert the algebraic lower bound on $A_L$ (Lemma E.1) into Theorem 2.12.

nodes.name: Inequalities with algebraic coefficients
nodes.statement: Assume the same hypotheses as Theorem \ref{Main Theorem chapter 3}, and assume further that $L$ has algebraic coefficients with algebraic degree at most $k$. Let $H$ denote the maximum absolute value of all of the coefficients of all of the minimal polynomials of the coefficients of $L$. Then \[ T^{L}_{F,G,N}(f_1,\dots,f_{d})\ll_{c,C,\varepsilon,H} \rho^{\Omega(1)} + N^{-\Omega(1)}\rho^{-O_k(1)}.\]
nodes.section: 2.4 The main theorem and a partial converse
nodes.statement_short: For algebraic $L$, the Main Theorem error becomes $\rho^{\Omega(1)}+N^{-\Omega(1)}\rho^{-O_k(1)}$.
assumptions: Assume the same hypotheses as Theorem \ref{Main Theorem chapter 3}, and assume further that $L$ has algebraic coefficients with algebraic degree at most $k$. Let $H$ denote the maximum absolute value of all of the coefficients of all of the minimal polynomials of the coefficients of $L$.
conclusions: Then \[ T^{L}_{F,G,N}(f_1,\dots,f_{d})\ll_{c,C,\varepsilon,H} \rho^{\Omega(1)} + N^{-\Omega(1)}\rho^{-O_k(1)}.\]
nodes.label: Corollary algebraic

nodes.name: Partial converse to the Main Theorem
nodes.statement: Let $m,d$ be natural numbers, satisfying $d\geqslant m+2$, and let $\varepsilon, c, C$ be positive constants. For each natural number $N$, let $L = L(N):\mathbb{R}^{d}\longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^m$ be a linear map satisfying $\Vert L\Vert_\infty\leqslant C$. Let $F:\mathbb{R}^d\longrightarrow [0,1]$ denote the indicator function of $[1,N]^d$ and $G:\mathbb{R}^m\longrightarrow [0,1]$ denote the indicator function of $[-\varepsilon,\varepsilon]^m$. Assume further that $\operatorname{dist}(L,V_{\operatorname{rank}}(m,d))\geqslant c$ and that $T_{F,G,N}^L(1,\dots,1)\gg_{c,C,\varepsilon} 1$ for large enough $N$. Suppose that $$\liminf\limits_{N\rightarrow\infty}\operatorname{dist}(L,V^*_{\operatorname{degen}}(m,d)) = 0.$$ Let $s$ be a natural number, let $H:\mathbb{R}_{>0}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}_{>0}$ be any function satisfying $H(\rho) = \kappa(\rho)$, and for each $N$ let $E_{\rho}(N)$ denote some error term depending on a parameter $\rho$ and satisfying $E_{\rho}(N) = o_{\rho}(1)$ as $N \rightarrow \infty$. Then one can find infinitely many natural numbers $N$ such that there exist functions $f_1,\dots,f_d:[N]\rightarrow [-1,1]$ and some $\rho$ at most $1$ such that both \[ \min_j\Vert f_j\Vert_{U^{s+1}[N]}\leqslant\rho\] and \begin{equation} \vert T_{F,G,N}^L(f_1,\dots,f_d)\vert > H(\rho)+E_{\rho}(N). \end{equation}
nodes.section: 2.4 The main theorem and a partial converse
nodes.statement_short: If $L$ approaches the dual degeneracy variety, no Gowers norm can control the weighted inequality count.
assumptions: Let $m,d$ be natural numbers, satisfying $d\geqslant m+2$, and let $\varepsilon, c, C$ be positive constants. For each natural number $N$, let $L = L(N):\mathbb{R}^{d}\longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^m$ be a linear map satisfying $\Vert L\Vert_\infty\leqslant C$. Let $F:\mathbb{R}^d\longrightarrow [0,1]$ denote the indicator function of $[1,N]^d$ and $G:\mathbb{R}^m\longrightarrow [0,1]$ denote the indicator function of $[-\varepsilon,\varepsilon]^m$. Assume further that $\operatorname{dist}(L,V_{\operatorname{rank}}(m,d))\geqslant c$ and that $T_{F,G,N}^L(1,\dots,1)\gg_{c,C,\varepsilon} 1$ for large enough $N$. Suppose that $$\liminf\limits_{N\rightarrow\infty}\operatorname{dist}(L,V^*_{\operatorname{degen}}(m,d)) = 0.$$ Let $s$ be a natural number, let $H:\mathbb{R}_{>0}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}_{>0}$ be any function satisfying $H(\rho) = \kappa(\rho)$, and for each $N$ let $E_{\rho}(N)$ denote some error term depending on a parameter $\rho$ and satisfying $E_{\rho}(N) = o_{\rho}(1)$ as $N \rightarrow \infty$.
conclusions: Then one can find infinitely many natural numbers $N$ such that there exist functions $f_1,\dots,f_d:[N]\rightarrow [-1,1]$ and some $\rho$ at most $1$ such that both \[ \min_j\Vert f_j\Vert_{U^{s+1}[N]}\leqslant\rho\] and \begin{equation} \vert T_{F,G,N}^L(f_1,\dots,f_d)\vert > H(\rho)+E_{\rho}(N). \end{equation}
nodes.label: Converse to main theorem

nodes.name: Conclusion of the converse theorem
nodes.statement: \vert T_{F,G,N}^L(f_1,\dots,f_d)\vert > H(\rho)+E_{\rho}(N).
nodes.section: 2.4 The main theorem and a partial converse
nodes.label: conclusion of converse theorem

nodes.name: Rational-relation example count
nodes.statement: T_{F,G,N}^L(f_1,\dots,f_4) = \frac{1}{N^2} \sum\limits_{ \substack{ \mathbf{n} \in \mathbb{Z}^4 \\ \Vert L\mathbf{n}\Vert_\infty \leqslant 10 \\ (\begin{smallmatrix}5 & 1 \end{smallmatrix})L\mathbf{n} = -1,0,1}} \Big(\prod\limits_{j=1}^4 f_j(n_j)\Big)F(\mathbf{n}).

nodes.name: Hoped-for kappa(delta) perturbation
nodes.statement: \vert T_{F,G,N}^L(f_1,\dots,f_4) - T_{F,\widetilde{G},N}^L(f_1,\dots,f_4)\vert = \kappa(\delta).
nodes.label: kappa delta

nodes.name: Cut range of summation
nodes.statement: T_{F, \widetilde{G},N}^L(f_1,\dots,f_4) \approx \frac{1}{N^2} \sum\limits_{\substack{\mathbf{n} \in \mathbb{Z}^4 \\ \Vert L \mathbf{n}\Vert_\infty \leqslant 10 - \delta \\ (\begin{smallmatrix}5 & 1 \end{smallmatrix})L\mathbf{n} = 0}}\Big(\prod\limits_{j=1}^4 f_j(n_j)\Big) F(\mathbf{n}).

nodes.name: Reparametrised expression via Xi
nodes.statement: \frac{1}{N^2} \sum\limits_{\mathbf{m} \in \mathbb{Z}^3 } \Big( \prod\limits_{j=1}^4 f_j(\Xi(\mathbf{m})_j+ \widetilde{\mathbf{r}}_j) \Big) F(\Xi(\mathbf{m}) + \widetilde{\mathbf{r}})1_{[-10,10]^2}(L(\Xi\mathbf{m} + \widetilde{\mathbf{r}}))

nodes.name: Heuristic transfer to real solution density
nodes.statement: \widetilde{T}_{F,G,N}^L(\widetilde{f_1},\dots,\widetilde{f_d}) &= \frac{1}{N^{d-m}} \sum\limits_{ \mathbf{n} \in \mathbb{Z}^d} \Big(\prod\limits_{j=1}^d f_j(n_j)\Big) \int\limits_{\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^d} F(\mathbf{y}) G(L\mathbf{y}) 1_{[-\eta,\eta]^d}(\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{n}) \, d\mathbf{y} \nonumber \\ &\approx \frac{1}{N^{d-m}} \sum\limits_{ \mathbf{n} \in \mathbb{Z}^d} \Big(\prod\limits_{j=1}^d f_j(n_j)\Big) F(\mathbf{n}) G(L\mathbf{n}) \int\limits_{\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^d} 1_{[-\eta,\eta]^d}(\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{n}) \, d\mathbf{y} \nonumber \\ & \approx (2 \eta)^dT_{F,G,N}^L(f_1,\dots,f_d),
nodes.label: Lipschitz is needed equation

nodes.name: Real solution density bounded by kernel integral
nodes.statement: \vert\widetilde{T}_{F,G,N}^L(\widetilde{f_1},\dots,\widetilde{f_d}) \vert \ll_G \frac{1}{N^{d-m}} \int\limits_{ \substack{ \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^d \\ L\mathbf\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}}} \Big(\prod\limits_{j=1}^d \widetilde{f_j} (x_j)\Big) F(\mathbf{x}) \, d \mu(\mathbf{x}),
